statements.quote: Training and inference are the *same function* — the same weights, the same attention, the same layers — but they are **different forms of computation**, and the difference is the load-bearing fact of the whole serving economy.
In [Attention](attentionlab.php) you saw the mechanism; in [Inference optimization](inference_optimization.php) and [Production serving](production_serving.php) you will meet the tricks.

This chapter gives them the *reason*: why a model that took minutes to train on a batch takes *seconds per token* to serve, and why "how many tokens per second?" and "how many users at once?" are two different questions with two different answers.
During **training**, the model sees the *whole* sequence at once — a prompt and its target, as a dense block of $T$ tokens processed in parallel.
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: That parallelism is what makes a GPU fast: a big block of tokens is a dense matrix multiply, and dense matrix multiplies are exactly the work a GPU's arithmetic units are built for.
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: Training is **compute-bound** — the bottleneck is the sheer number of floating-point operations.
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: **Inference** is different.
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: Generation is *autoregressive*: you produce **one token at a time**, and each new token must attend to every token that came before it.
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: There is no "batch of $T$ new tokens" to parallelize — there is exactly one.
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: So the question at each step is no longer "how many multiplies?" (just one token's worth) but "how much *data* do I have to move to compute this one token?" And the answer is: *a lot* — the entire model's weights, plus every past token's attention state.
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: That makes decode **memory-bandwidth-bound**: the arithmetic units sit mostly idle while the memory bus is the thing keeping up.

statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel (a dense, compute-bound block).
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: Decode then appends one token at a time, and every step must read the entire KV-cache that has grown up to that point (a memory-bound step).
statements.section: Training runs over a batch; inference runs over a stream

statements.quote: Attention is $O(T^2)$ in the naive reading: token $i$ attends to all $i$ preceding tokens.
statements.section: The KV-cache: stop recomputing the past

statements.quote: If you recomputed that from scratch for every new token, generation would be catastrophically slow — the cost would grow quadratically with length.
statements.section: The KV-cache: stop recomputing the past

statements.quote: The **KV-cache** is the fix: the keys and values for each past token are computed *once* and **stored**, so when the next token arrives its attention *reuses* the cached keys and values instead of recomputing them.
statements.section: The KV-cache: stop recomputing the past

statements.quote: You trade memory for arithmetic: the cache grows by one key and one value per layer, per head, per new token — **linear** in sequence length — and decode stays $O(T)$ rather than $O(T^2)$ per step.
statements.section: The KV-cache: stop recomputing the past

statements.quote: That cache is also, quietly, the most important *physical* object in serving.
statements.section: The KV-cache: stop recomputing the past

statements.quote: It is where the memory goes as context length grows, and it is the thing the memory-bound decode step has to move.
statements.section: The KV-cache: stop recomputing the past

statements.quote: Everything below — why long contexts are expensive, why people quantize, why they build PagedAttention — is a consequence of that cache.
statements.section: The KV-cache: stop recomputing the past

statements.quote: Because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, its cost is dominated by *how many bytes you read*, not how many flops you do.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: And you read two things: the model weights (once per step) and the KV-cache (which grows with context).
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: Three consequences follow, and they shape the entire serving industry (\cite[Pope et al., 2022]{pope2022scaling}).
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: **Long contexts are expensive, per token.** A 32k-token context means every decode step reads a 32k-token cache.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: The per-token cost of *decoding* climbs with the length of what is already in the window — which is why "how long can it read?" and "how fast does it answer?" are coupled, and why the [context window](contextwindows.php) is a cost dial, not just a feature.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: **The optimizations are all about moving fewer bytes.** **Quantization** shrinks the bytes of both weights and cache (lower precision, fewer bits to move).
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: **FlashAttention** (\cite[Dao et al., 2022]{flashattention2022}) reorders the computation so the attention matrix is never materialized in memory, cutting the memory traffic of the attention itself.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: And **PagedAttention** (\cite[Kwon et al., vLLM (2023)]{vllm2023}) manages the KV-cache like an operating system manages virtual memory — in fixed-size *blocks* — so you do not reserve a worst-case contiguous chunk per sequence and waste half the memory to fragmentation.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: **Throughput and concurrency are different numbers.** "Tokens per second" is the speed of *one* stream — a property of the memory-bound decode step.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: "How many *users* at once" is a property of *how many KV-caches fit in memory* — a capacity question.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: Continuous batching interleaves many sequences' decode steps so the (memory-bound) hardware is kept busy with more than one stream, trading a little latency-per-stream for a lot more total users.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: A serving system is a machine for managing that trade-off, and the KV-cache is the working set it manages.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: > The reason the "optimizations" in the next chapters work is the reason a single token takes as long as it does: inference is not a smaller version of training.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

statements.quote: It is a *different bottleneck* — one where moving bytes, not computing them, is the scarce resource, and where a linearly growing cache is the object of all the attention.
statements.section: Why the two regimes set the economics
